A case constructed for teaching: the underlying CT is real (public archive) and the aorta was normal; the flap, false lumen and re-entry were added by computer while preserving the image noise. The small mass of the right kidney, by contrast, is real.
Dissection is recognized by the intimal flap (a thin line, hypodense relative to the opacified blood) that separates a true lumen and a false lumen. The true lumen is usually smaller, compressed by the false lumen, sometimes denser and in continuity with the undissected aorta; the false lumen is larger, may opacify less or later and may contain thrombus; often the false lumen wraps around the true lumen (beak sign) and the branches arise from one or the other.
Classification: Stanford A if it involves the ascending aorta (regardless of the location of the entry tear: cardiac surgical emergency), Stanford B if it does not; DeBakey I (ascending and beyond), II (ascending only), III (descending only). Here the field of view starts below the heart: the ascending aorta and arch are not seen, so the type cannot be stated. This is the key point of the case: an abdominal CT showing a dissection must be completed immediately with a CT angiogram of the thoracic aorta (preferably ECG-gated), without making the patient wait.
In the report: proximal and distal extent, maximum diameter, entry and re-entry tears, from which lumen the celiac axis, SMA and renal arteries arise, perfusion of bowel, kidneys and limbs (malperfusion), signs of rupture (bloody pleural or pericardial effusion, periaortic hematoma).
Pitfalls: pulsation artifacts in the ascending aortic root; intramural hematoma (no flap, best seen without contrast); in too early a phase the false lumen can appear thrombosed.
Incidental finding: the small mass of the right kidney is described and deferred until after the emergency.
